claims.text: The target eutectic high-entropy alloy contains dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries.
Internal lamellar-colony boundaries act as crack-initiation sites during room-temperature tensile loading.
Selective annealing after trace Hf addition will promote Hf segregation to interphase or colony boundaries.
Boundary segregation of Hf will form ultra-thin amorphous intergranular films at lamellar-colony and phase boundaries.
The amorphous intergranular films will blunt boundary stress concentrations and crack tips.
The amorphous intergranular films will absorb and emit dislocations.
The amorphous intergranular films will promote local plasticity at boundaries.
Crack-tip blunting and enhanced local plasticity will delay crack initiation.
Trace Hf addition plus selective annealing will simultaneously improve tensile strength and room-temperature ductility relative to the unmodified alloy.
The modified alloy will have a higher tensile yield strength than the unmodified baseline.
The modified alloy will have a higher ultimate tensile strength than the unmodified baseline.
The modified alloy will have greater uniform elongation than the unmodified baseline.
The modified alloy will have greater overall tensile ductility than the unmodified baseline.
A bounded optimal Hf-concentration and processing window exists in which beneficial amorphous films form without detrimental interfacial changes.
Below the optimal Hf or processing range, insufficient amorphous intergranular film formation will occur.
Above the optimal range, excessive amorphous-film thickness may soften interfaces and reduce mechanical performance.
Higher Hf additions can cause secondary intermetallic-phase precipitation.
Secondary-phase precipitation above the optimal Hf range may reduce the target alloy's mechanical performance.
